additions.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 5.1: Skills, knowledge and expertise (competent employees rule)
additions.locator: SYSC 5.1.1R (text shown as in force from 23/10/2025)
additions.quote: A firm must employ personnel with the skills, knowledge and expertise necessary for the discharge of the responsibilities allocated to them.
additions.why: A binding UK rule on the competence of the person: a regulated firm that allocates oversight of an AI system to someone must be able to show that person has the skills for it. Limits: applies to FCA-authorised firms only; a general rule that does not mention AI or human oversight; the Handbook page says SYSC 5.1 was last updated on 09/12/2025.

additions.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
additions.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
additions.quote: Roles and responsibilities should be allocated to staff with appropriate skills and experience to ensure the MRM framework operates effectively.
additions.why: The prudential regulator's expectation that those who challenge and monitor models have documented skills, experience, independence and seniority for the role; Principle 4 adds independent, effective challenge. Limits: banks, building societies and designated investment firms only; covers models generally, including AI; in effect from 17 May 2024.

additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), via The National Archives Find Case Law
additions.quote: We do not consider the "human failsafe" is sufficient to discharge the PSED.
additions.why: The Court of Appeal declined to treat a human check on each facial recognition match as an answer to the duty to investigate possible bias in the software, noting that human beings also make mistakes. Shows that the presence of an overseer does not by itself discharge the organisation's own duty. Limits: decided on the public sector equality duty and police use of live facial recognition; not a ruling on reviewer training.

additions.title: Institutionalised distrust and human oversight of artificial intelligence: towards a democratic design of AI governance under the European Union AI Act
additions.quote: They may be lacking in competence or be harmfully incentivised.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Names the two failure points this criterion tests, competence and incentives, and argues the EU Act says little on how to make oversight effective; proposes principles that assume overseers are fallible. Limits: legal and conceptual analysis, not an empirical study; written about the EU Act before its 2026 amendment; abstract was the passage read.

additions.title: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision-Making: "Automation Bias" and "Selective Adherence" to Algorithmic Advice
additions.publisher: Alon-Barkat and Busuioc; Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory (author copy on arXiv, v3)
additions.quote: We find a stronger propensity for adherence when the advice is aligned with group stereotypes
additions.why: Three experiments (605, 904 and 1,345 participants, the last with civil servants) on how decision-makers treat algorithmic advice. A caution against a single story: the authors did not find automation bias, but in one study found advice was followed more readily when it matched stereotypes. Limits: the Netherlands; survey experiments, not live casework; the arXiv listing says it was published in the journal in 2022, and the author copy was read, not the publisher's.

additions.title: Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction
additions.publisher: Elish; Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, Vol. 5 (2019)
additions.quote: responsibility for an action may be misattributed to a human actor who had limited control over the behavior of an automated or autonomous system
additions.why: Open access journal article behind the brief's point that the overseer carries blame for outcomes they could not change: the nearest human absorbs moral and legal responsibility when an automated system fails. Limits: case studies of accidents (aviation, self-driving cars) and their media coverage, not a measured effect; US; abstract was the passage read.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.locator: Suggested action MS-4.2-004; GOVERN 3.2 on roles for human-AI configurations and oversight
additions.quote: Monitor and document instances where human operators or other systems override the GAI's decisions.
additions.why: A standard-setter's version of the measure the framework's higher levels expect: record and evaluate overrides. The profile also treats automation bias and over-reliance as a named risk ('Human-AI Configuration'). Limits: voluntary; US; generative AI only; a different document from the AI RMF 1.0 already on the list.

brief_check: No contradiction. Two refinements: (1) the brief says UK law 'says little about the person'; for FCA-authorised firms SYSC 5.1.1R is a binding competence rule, though it is general and does not mention AI. (2) One peer-reviewed study read (Alon-Barkat and Busuioc, 2022) did not find automation bias in its experiments, so 'approves what the system proposes' is a risk, not a universal finding; the brief's figure sentence rests on Green (2022) and is unaffected.
